Final Project and Final Assessment (Part 3: Sessions 25 and 26)

The course's capstone, closing Part 3 and the whole course. The final project is Lesson 11.1's: each learner chooses one of seven client briefs (or their own idea within the size rules), plans it on the kit's worksheet, builds it types first from the kit's starter in about 25 hours over three to five weeks, launches a demo build on a free static host, has it reviewed by a peer and shows it in Session 26. The source is the final-project kit (downloads/final-project-kit/: README, worksheet, seven briefs, rubric, peer review, starter). This section adds only the instructor's side: the timeline, milestone check-ins, scoring notes for each rubric row, the Session 26 run-sheet, a scoring sheet, how results are recorded, and the course's written final assessment (24 items on all three parts, with its key). The rubric below is the kit's rubric.md, unchanged.

Size rules for an own idea (Lesson 11.1): 2 to 4 domain types with at least one union of literal types; 5 to 9 routes including a detail page with a parameter, a not-found page and a list whose search or filter lives in the address; at least one form with a schema and a rule only the server can check; at least one change saved through a mutation; a demo build with its mock API on a free static host, or a real API with its hosting and monthly cost written down; no real payments, no stored passwords, no live chat or notifications (demo sign-in with sample accounts is fine).

If Session 26 must follow Session 25 within a week

The project cannot be finished in a week (Lesson 11.1: about 25 more hours, usually 20 to 30, over three to five weeks). Run Session 26 as a progress showcase (Milestones 1 to 3, the same five-minute format with "what's next" stretched) and the written final assessment as planned, then set a final evidence date two to three weeks later and score the rubric from that evidence. Say so in Session 25.

The rubric (Lesson 11.1's rubric.md, verbatim)

#CriterionNot yet (0)Meets (1)Strong (2)
1Plan (worksheet)Sections missing, or copied from Shoreline Crew HQ without thoughtEvery section filled for this brief; decisions have reasons; time log keptTrade-offs argued with evidence (demo vs real API, state placement, one page vs steps); estimate vs actual hours reflected on
2Types and dataany, type assertions (as) to silence errors, or API data used before it is checkedDomain types in one file; unions for statuses with complete Record tables; every API answer checked by a guard or schema; npx tsc -b cleanComputed values never stored; request types made from the domain types with utility types; a type error found and fixed early is written up in the journal
3Routes and screensMissing pages, dead links, or a blank screen on a reload or an unknown addressEvery route in the worksheet works; a layout with a skip link; a not-found page and an error page; shareable views keep their state in the addressLazy routes where the worksheet planned them; guards or loaders for pages some people may not open
4States and messagesA page that shows nothing (or "undefined") while loading, after an error, or when a list is emptyLoading, error (with Try again), empty and not-found states written for people; focus moves to the new page and to the first problem in a formPartial failures handled with boundaries; messages tested with server overrides in Vitest
5Server data and stateServer data copied into useState; lists that don't update after a changeTanStack Query factories with keys general to specific; changes through mutations that invalidate the right keys; every piece of state where the placement table saysAn optimistic change with a rollback where the brief needs it, tested; no app-wide store entries that could be derived or live in the address
6FormsFields without labels, or errors that only show in the consoleOne schema for each form's rules and types; field errors under the fields and linked with aria-describedby; the server's own rules shown under the fieldField arrays or steps where the brief needs them, with an error summary; input and output types used deliberately
7Accessibility and performanceKeyboard traps, invisible focus, contrast failures, missing alt textaxe 0 violations on every page type at 1280 and 390 px in light and dark; keyboard walk passes; the build table measured against the budgetA budget test (Lesson 10.1) or the forms chunk kept off the first page, measured; a screen reader check written up
8Tests and CINo tests, or tests that failUnit and component tests for the helpers, the mock API's rules and the main forms; at least one Playwright journey with axe; npm run lint at 0 warnings; both CI jobs green on the latest commitThe "must not happen" test from the worksheet; a regression test for a bug you actually had
9Launch and securityNot public; or a secret, an API key or .env.local in Git or in the buildPublic HTTPS link on a free static host; _redirects and _headers live; a demo banner that says what the demo is; every line of the live launch checklist ticked or notedHosting terms and monthly cost written down; the README has the link, a screenshot, how to run it and the main decisions
10Review and reflectionNo peer review given or receivedPeer review given with the checklist; every point answered (fixed, or why not)Review comments specific and kind, with steps to reproduce; a reflection on what you would do differently

Total ____ / 20. The project is complete when no row is "not yet"; "not yet" is not a failing grade, it is the list of what to do next; "strong" rows are what make it a portfolio piece.

Scoring notes for instructors

For each row: where the evidence is, how to check "meets" quickly, and how to tell "meets" from "strong" when it is close. These notes never change what a row asks for; when they seem to, the rubric wins.

RowEvidenceHow to check (meets)Meets or strong?
1. Plan (worksheet)worksheet.md in the repository: the charter (section 0), the time log (section 11), the risks (section 12).Every section names this brief's things, not Shoreline Crew's; decisions have a reason; the time log has actual hours, not only estimates. The evidence check's row 1 lines are the quick test.Strong needs evidence behind a trade-off (why a demo build and not a real API, why one page and not steps, a state placement argued) and a sentence comparing estimated and actual hours.
2. Types and datasrc/api/types.ts, the client's guards, the schemas; npx tsc -b on a fresh clone.Domain types in one file; every status a union with a complete Record label table; API answers checked by a guard or a schema before use; search the code for any and as and read each hit.Strong: computed values (totals, overdue, available) never stored; request types built with Pick / Omit / Partial; the journal names a type error found early.
3. Routes and screensThe live link and worksheet section 2 (routes).Open every planned route; reload a detail page; open /no-such-page (their not-found page); a skip link; a filtered view keeps its state in the address after a reload.Strong: lazy routes where the worksheet planned them; a loader or guard for pages some people may not open.
4. States and messagesThe live app with its awkward sample record; a search with no results; the mock API's 404 and 500 answers.Loading, error with Try again, empty and not-found states written for people; focus moves to <main> on a new page and to the first problem in a form.Strong: a partial failure handled by a boundary while the rest of the page works; the messages tested with server.use(...) overrides in Vitest.
5. Server data and statesrc/api/queries.ts, mutations.ts; worksheet section 4 (state placement).Query key factories, general to specific; every change through a mutation that invalidates the right keys (make a change: the list updates); no server data copied into useState.Strong: an optimistic change with a rollback, tested (a 409 or 500 from the mock API puts it back); the app-wide store holds nothing that could be derived or live in the address.
6. FormsThe main forms in the live app; src/api/schemas.ts.Submit empty and wrong values: field errors under the fields, linked with aria-describedby; the server-only rule's message (the mock API's 409 or 400) under its field; one schema per form for rules and types.Strong: a field array or steps where the brief needs them, with an error summary; input and output types used on purpose (z.input / z.output).
7. Accessibility and performanceThe e2e axe test and its results; the build table (npm run build); worksheet sections 7 and 8.axe 0 violations on every page type at 1280 and 390 px, light and dark (the starter's e2e shows how); a keyboard walk: skip link, every control, focus always visible; the build measured against the worksheet's budget.Strong: a budget test (Lesson 10.1) or the forms chunk measured off the first page; a written screen reader check (which reader, which page, what was fixed).
8. Tests and CIThe repository's tests; the GitHub Actions tab on the latest commit.Unit and component tests for the helpers, the mock API's rules and the main forms; at least one Playwright journey with axe; npm run lint at 0 warnings; both CI jobs green on the LATEST commit (open the run).Strong: the "must not happen" test from worksheet section 9; a regression test for a bug the learner actually had (the history or the journal shows it).
9. Launch and securityThe live link; curl -I on it; .env.example; the README; the learner's live launch checklist (Lesson 10.2).Public HTTPS on a free static host; _redirects and _headers live (X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, X-Frame-Options; /assets/ immutable); a demo banner that says what the demo is; no .env.local, key or secret in Git or in a VITE_ variable.Strong: the host's terms and monthly cost written down; a README with the link, a screenshot, how to run it and the main decisions.
10. Review and reflectionThe review given (with peer-review.md), the review received and the author's answers.A review given with the checklist; every received point answered with a fix (and its commit) or a sentence on why not.Strong: comments that are specific and kind, with steps to reproduce; a reflection on what the learner would do differently (the journal is a good source).
Scoring habits
  • Score from evidence you opened, not from the demo's polish: a smooth five minutes can hide a red CI run, and a nervous demo can hide excellent work.
  • Self, peer and instructor scores differ by 2 on a row? Talk before you record it; usually one of you missed a piece of evidence.
  • A row is "not yet" only when its "meets" column is not met. Write the one sentence that would move it to "meets" next to the 0.
  • The scope is the learner's: do not score down a must-have the charter put out of scope with a reason.
  • The evidence check (labs/module-26/showcase-preflight/evidence_check.mjs) reads files only; it is a list of missing evidence, never a score. As downloaded, the kit's starter gets six FIX lines (names, the worksheet, the example Item, the README): a project that still shows them is not ready to be scored.

Question bank
  • Which value do you compute instead of storing, and why?
  • What happens when I reload a detail page, or open an address that does not exist?
  • Which rule does only your mock API check, and where is its test?
  • What did you put out of scope, and what would it take to add it?
  • Where were your estimates furthest from the actual hours, and why?
  • What did your peer review find that you had missed?
Class sizeFormat
Up to 12Two rounds of six 7-minute slots, as above
13 to 18Three rounds of 5-minute slots (4 demo, 1 question; the rest on cards); the evidence results read out in 2 minutes
19 or moreA gallery: half the room presents at stations for 25 minutes while the other half visits, then swap; you visit every station for a 4-minute demo. Or a second showcase block before Session 26
If…Then
The network failsThe learner's screenshots or a recording; the evidence check and the peer review show what the live checks found
A project is not liveDemo npm run dev:demo on the laptop; row 9 is "not yet" with a plan, nothing else changes
A learner is absentA recorded five-minute demo sent by the evidence date counts as the showcase
A demo overrunsThe timekeeper stands at 5:00 and 7:00; the rest goes on cards

Recording results

  • Final project: complete when no rubric row is at 0 (the rubric's own definition), by the end of the resubmission window; record the total out of 20 and the rows at "strong" for references and portfolio notes.
  • Written final assessment: 27 points (21 multiple-choice items at 1 point, 3 short answers at 2 points). Pass mark: 19 (19 of 27, 70 %). Below it: go through the wrong items with the learner and offer a parallel retake of your choice (the same lessons, other items).
  • Course complete = final project complete AND the written final assessment passed: the final project complete under Lesson 11.1's rubric, and at least 19 of 27 points on the written final. The Part 1 and Part 2 results (above) are the results when a part runs on its own.
  • Late work: the resubmission window is the late window. After it, "not yet" rows stay "not yet" and the learner gets a written list of what would complete them.

Part 1: TypeScript and React Foundations (Sessions 1 to 9): key
F1 · 1 point
node spots.ts prints this for a file with a typo in a property name. Which tool would have named the typo before the file ran?
Weekend Cove Cleanup: NaN spots left
A) Node.js, with a warning on the next run
B) The browser's console
C) The TypeScript compiler (tsc) or the editor
D) npm install
Why: Node runs a .ts file by stripping its types and never checks them; the editor and tsc read the types first (TS2551, with a Did you mean). Running is not checking. Lesson 1.1.
F2 · 1 point
The app's build script is tsc -b && vite build. What happens to vite build when tsc finds one type error?
A) It never runs
B) It runs and builds the files without errors
C) It builds everything and prints a warning
D) It runs first, then tsc reports
